articles.summary: Most small businesses in the Philippines fund a client's job before the client pays for it. A caterer buys ingredients and books servers weeks before the event. A furniture shop orders plywood and hardware before the first cut is made. The full payment usually comes at the end, and for corporate clients, that can mean another 30 to 60 days after the work is delivered. A downpayment is the simplest way to close part of that gap. articles.summary: In most hotels, ordering food to your room still runs on a phone call and a printed menu. Someone writes the order down, the kitchen gets a ticket, and the charge is posted to the room to be settled at checkout. That process works, which is probably why few operators look closely at what it costs them. articles.summary: A Philippine business selling to someone in another country has more ways to get paid than it did ten years ago, and most of them work. Access is no longer the problem. The work now is picking a route that matches how the customer wants to pay, then handling the things that go differently once money crosses a border: who sets the exchange rate, why cards get declined more often, what the fees are, and what happens when a customer in another time zone disputes a charge.
